newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Howard rejects Stokes' claim of a deal.
newsitem.headline: Howard rejects Stokes' claim of a deal.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard rejected on Friday as "silly and erroneous" a claim by Seven Network Ltd Chairman Kerry Stokes that Howard had done a deal to deliver John Fairfax Holdings Ltd to billionaire businessman Kerry Packer.
"I rejectly completely any suggestion of a deal as a silly, erroneous and quite dishonourable claim," Howard told a news conference in Sydney.
Earlier on Friday Stokes told Reuters in an interview Howard had done what he called a disgraceful deal that would deliver Fairfax to Packer.

Howard described the allegation that he had done a deal to allow Packer to take over Fairfax in exchange for political support as a tiresome one that was started by Labor Prime Minister Paul Keating on an overseas trip before the 1996 election.
"I'm on the record over a period of 10 years as being opposed to the cross-media restrictions," Howard said.
The cross-media rules set up by the former Labor government stop a television station owner from owning more than 15 percent of a major newspaper in the same city or vice-versa.
These cross-media rules prevent the Kerry Packer-controlled Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd from increasing its 12 percent Fairfax stake and taking over the publisher.
The government is currently reviewing the cross-media rules and is widely expected to remove them, prompting a Packer bid for Fairfax.

Stokes' claim arose after a report in the Australian Financial Review that said Howard had tried to broker an arrangement whereby News Corp Ltd would be allowed to raise its stake in the Seven Network if News supported an easing of cross-media rules to allow a Packer takeover of Fairfax.
The Financial Review said Howard's plan fell through last week when News rejected one part of it which would have seen News sell some of its Australian newspapers to a new owner.
Howard said at the news conference that he had not tried to broker such an arrangement.
He said News had proposed to him that the government lift its 15 percent limit on foreign shareholdings so that News could increase its Seven stake from its current 14 percent.
It had also been suggested that News would sell off some of its newspaper holdings so that News' total holding in Australian media did not rise, Howard said.
He said this arrangement had not gone ahead.
Asked if he approved of such an arrangement.
Howard said that Stokes did not want the cross media rules changed and all media proprietors made statements in their own interests.
"Every media proprietor in Australia is pushing his or her own barrow," he said.
